notes: "A big wave came. Harvey fell into the cold sea!" — other levels say the ship rolled. This does not contradict them (the sea was rough), and the A1 quiz key fits the A1 text.
"Long Jack showed him the ropes." — this is an idiom, but the literal reading is also correct here, so it works at A1.
Leaving out the stolen-money scene simplifies the story, but "Disko did not believe Harvey's story" still makes sense.

"He became strong, brown and polite." — 'brown' (meaning sunburned) may confuse some A2 readers. 'strong, sunburned and polite' is an option, but Kipling uses 'brown' and the meaning is clear in context.
"They were full of sorrow." is a little literary for A2. 'They were very sad' would be simpler. This is a taste note only.
"The work was harder than anything Harvey knew." — 'had ever known' is more natural. Perfect tenses are allowed at B1.
"In his opinion, the fall hurt the boy's head" — 'had hurt' reads better. Minor.
"Take me back to land now, and he will pay you well" uses imperative + and + will, not a formal conditional, so it is acceptable at B1. No passive found.
The quiz 2 key paraphrases the text ('too strange to invent' vs. 'too strange to be invented'). This is fine.

Fidelity is strong: the $10.50 wage, the lost roll of money, Dan's half-belief, the fog and the liner, the private car crossing in under four days, Mr. Cheyne's story of his own hard youth, four years of college, and Dan's place on a Cheyne ship are all in the novel. Disko's blow to Harvey's nose is correctly softened for a 4+ audience.

"On one morning a fog settled ... so close that they glimpsed lit windows and passengers at dinner" — a careful reader may stop at 'dinner' in a morning scene. The period meaning (midday dinner) and an all-day fog make it defensible. Suggested fix: 'One morning a fog settled...' and '...glimpsed lit windows and passengers on deck' (or set the fog in the evening).
"On one morning" — 'One morning' is more idiomatic.
The prose is literary and not padded. The fog reflection (Harvey was once one of those careless passengers) adds real C1 depth that follows the novel's themes.

summary: All five levels follow Kipling's main events in order: the fall from the liner, Manuel's rescue, Disko's disbelief and the job offer, Dan's friendship, the education at sea, the fog and liner, the return to Gloucester, the parents' record train journey, Disko's admission, Harvey going to college and Dan's place on a Cheyne ship. Grammar matches each level and the quiz keys are unambiguous. Disko striking Harvey and the cigar-induced sickness are softened in a way that keeps the content 4+ safe. Only minor wording notes remain, such as the C1 'passengers at dinner' in a morning fog.
